discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Upper level low dissipating over Oregon today. Building upper level ridge offshore moving over the area tonight and remaining over Western Washington through Friday night. Ridge gets pinched off Saturday with a weak system moving into the area Saturday night and Sunday. Warm front brushing the area Monday with the trailing cold front arriving Tuesday. Next system reaching the area Wednesday night into Thanksgiving day.
hydrology: No river flooding expected in the next 7 days.

sections.title: Update
paragraphs: An upper-low center remains positioned over Oregon as a few showers stream over the southern WA Cascades. This activity will dissipate before reaching the lowlands as conditions are favored to remain dry today. The main concern is fog this morning as areas across the Chehalis River valley, South Sound, and Snohomish County have dealt with visibility less than a mile. Lingering fog should give way to mostly clear skies by the afternoon. High temperatures this will top out in the upper 40s to near 50 F. The previous discussion is below along with an updated aviation section:

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Upper level low dissipating over Oregon today. Building upper level ridge offshore moving over the area tonight and remaining over Western Washington through Friday night. Ridge gets pinched off Saturday with a weak system moving into the area Saturday night and Sunday. Warm front brushing the area Monday with the trailing cold front arriving Tuesday. Next system reaching the area Wednesday night into Thanksgiving day.

sections.title: Short term (today through Saturday)
paragraphs: Satellite imagery shows upper level low over Western Oregon with clouds spinning around the low over most of Western Washington. Doppler radar has a couple of light showers along the Strait of Juan de Fuca with another area of showers that are probably not getting to the ground near Bellingham. A little bit of clearing in the South Sound allowed fog to form with visibilities in Tacoma and Olympia under a mile. Temperatures at 3 AM/11Z were in the mid 30s to mid 40s.

Upper level low weakening and remaining over Western Oregon today. Could see some upslope showers near the Cascade crest but for the most part just a lot of cloud cover associated with the low at this point. Expecting a small increase in the fog coverage this morning. The layer is shallow so even with the cloud cover visibility restrictions going away by afternoon. At least mostly cloudy skies keeping highs a couple of degrees either side of 50.

Upper level low dissipating tonight. High amplitude upper level ridge offshore building into Northern British Columbia and the Yukon today will move east tonight with drying northerly flow aloft by early Friday morning. Light flow in the lower levels combining with the clearing skies to produce areas of fog early Friday morning with areas of freezing fog in the South Puget Sound and Southwest Interior. Lows in the upper 20s and 30s.

Upper level ridge remaining over Western Washington Friday with the ridge axis offshore and dry northerly flow aloft over the area. Light flow is the lower levels making for a tough call on when the fog will dissipate. Even though the layer is shallow could see areas of fog lasting into the early afternoon hours especially in the South Puget Sound. Highs in the mid 40s to lower 50s.

Upper level ridge axis moving inland Friday night with the next system moving inside of 130W by 12Z Saturday. System moving east Saturday pinching off the upper level ridge north of the area. Moving into the backside of the ridge along with the jet aimed into Northern California will weaken the system as it moves into Western Washington later Saturday. System will be weak enough to call the precipitation type showers. Snow levels dropping below the pass levels but at least during the day Saturday moisture looks somewhat limited for the Cascades keeping new snow amounts very light if any at all. Felton

sections.title: Long term (Saturday night through Wednesday)
paragraphs: Extended models in good agreement with upper low off the coast just spinning around Saturday night and Sunday before dissipating Sunday night. A couple of weak impulses spinning out of the low moving through Western Washington keeping a chance of showers in the forecast.

Warm front brushing the area Monday with the trailing cold front arriving Tuesday. Parent upper level low associated with the fronts moving north which will stretch out and weaken the cold front as in moves inland Tuesday night. Deep surface low, around 960 mb, also associated with the cold front but the low is far enough to the northwest to confine the windy conditions to the coast Tuesday and Tuesday night. Breezy conditions over the interior just ahead and with the frontal passage Tuesday night.

Another developing system right behind the cold front approaching the area Wednesday night. Will have to keep an eye on this one with some of the solutions indicating a much further east track than the low Tuesday night. There are some big differences, up to 15 mb, on the strength of the surface low. Right now most of the model solutions with the stronger low turn the low north near 130W late Wednesday into Thanksgiving which would minimize the impacts over the area.

In addition to all this we will be getting into the highest tides of the month next week. The combination of wind, high tides and low pressure will cause some coastal flooding problems beginning as early as Tuesday. Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: VFR this morning at the majority of terminals aside from LIFR fog at KHQM and KOLM. Otherwise, VFR conditions will prevail today with clouds and areas of fog scattering out by the afternoon. Northerly surface winds today will become southerly this afternoon. Mostly clear skies and light/calm winds will promote patchy fog development over the southern interior tonight into Friday morning.

KSEA...VFR with high clouds this morning will then scatter out this afternoon. Northeasterly winds 7-9 kt today,  transitioning more north-northwesterly this afternoon. Winds will decrease tonight to around 5 kt and become southeasterly. Model guidance hints at a 30% chance for MVFR cigs Friday morning after 12Z.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Seas this morning hovering between 10-11 feet will continue to subside today below 10 feet, allowing the Small Craft Advisory over the coastal waters to expire later this morning. Weak high pressure will build over the waters today through Friday, for generally benign marine conditions. The weather pattern will become more active again starting this weekend, with headlines likely continuing into next week. A low pressure system spinning offshore this weekend will bring elevated seas and winds to the waters. Latest probabilities for small craft winds over the coastal waters exceed 70%. There is a 50-80% for small craft winds through the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Additionally, models hint at 30-45% chance for gales over the outer coastal waters. Seas will build to 10-15 feet.

A stronger system will impact the waters Monday through Tuesday. Increased offshore winds are highly likely to bring additional headlines to the waters. Confidence continues to increase with the each model run for gales and storm force winds over the coastal waters. Latest model guidance highlights a 50-75% chance for gales over the coastal waters starting Monday morning. Winds will peak on Tuesday with high confidence (90% and higher) for gales and a 35-50% chance of storm force winds over the coastal waters. Moreover, there is a 65-75% chance for gales through the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and a slight chance (35%) for storm force winds through the Central and East Strait. Seas also continue to trend upwards with combined seas now approaching 20 feet over the outer coastal waters.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: A brief period of dry, calm weather will prevail today and Friday under transient high pressure before an active pattern returns this weekend. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain and mountain snow starting Saturday and continuing through next week. While exact details remain subject to ensemble spread, there is a low 5-10% probability of a stronger low tracking close enough to bring higher impact winds during the middle of next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A brief period of dry, calm weather will prevail today and Friday under transient high pressure before an active pattern returns this weekend. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain and mountain snow starting Saturday and continuing through next week. While exact details remain subject to ensemble spread, there is a low 5-10% probability of a stronger low tracking close enough to bring higher impact winds during the middle of next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Wednesday...Tranquil conditions across southwest Washington and northwest Oregon this morning will give way to a much more active and wet weather regime heading into the weekend and early next week. Transient shortwave ridging is building across the Pacific Northwest today, providing a much-needed break in precipitation following recent activity. However, this quiet interlude will be short- lived as a deep trough digs southeastward out of the Gulf of Alaska, driving our next incoming cold front toward the coast by Saturday. Active weather will then persist through Tuesday and Wednesday as multiple disturbances traverse the region, keeping overall confidence in daily mesoscale details low while highlighting an unsettled second half of the 7-day window.

the primary weather hazard of this forecast window centers on mountain pass travel and winter driving conditions starting this weekend. As the cold front pushes onshore Saturday, snow levels will drop rapidly down to 2000 to 3000 feet by Saturday evening across the Cascades. Ensemble guidance indicates a 60-80% probability for accumulating snow meeting or exceeding 2 inches at pass level (excluding Government Camp) over a 48-hour period, with significantly higher totals expected above 5000 feet. For Government Camp, there is only a 10-20% chance of accumulating snow meeting or exceeding 2 inches. Motorists traveling across the Cascades through Government Camp, Santiam Pass, and Willamette Pass should anticipate slick roads and winter driving conditions at times through the weekend and into early next week as snow levels fluctuate.

Secondary weather impacts will arrive in the form of widespread lowland rainfall and coastal precipitation starting late Friday night and Saturday. The cold front is expected to push onshore between 7 AM and noon Saturday, spreading steady rain inland by Saturday afternoon. Cumulative 48-hour QPF exceedance probabilities for amounts above 0.50 inches from Saturday through Monday highlight the coastal regions with the highest likelihood at 60-80%, followed by 40-60% across the Coast Range, and 20-40% across the interior Willamette Valley and I-5 corridor lowlands. Additional rounds of rain will follow on Tuesday and Wednesday, maintaining damp conditions across the lowlands.

Closer to the surface this morning and Friday morning, calmer sensible weather impacts will dominate the interior valleys. Clear breaks and moist ground conditions are fostering patchy fog and frost development across the I-5 corridor through southwest Washington, the Portland metro, and the Willamette Valley. Where fog and low stratus develop, expect slow burns with clearing windows generally occurring between 9-11 AM each morning, giving way to partial sunshine. Daytime high temperatures will hover near seasonal averages in the mid to upper 40s inland and lower 50s along the coast, with overnight lows dipping into the mid 30s.

Looking toward the extended period of early next week, ensemble cluster analysis for next Tuesday and Wednesday depicts considerable spread regarding the exact track and intensity of a subsequent digging trough. Cluster guidance shows a dominant majority scenario where the primary low develops well offshore, resulting in frontal rain and breezy conditions. However, a minority scenario continuing around 5-10% of members shows a deeper low tracking significantly closer to the coastline, which could introduce stronger, potentially damaging winds to parts of southwest Washington and northwest Oregon. Additionally, a secondary meso-low developing along the frontal boundary remains a plausible alternative that could focus heavier precipitation bands near the coast. Model trends over the coming days will be critical in resolving these finer-scale details. ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Friday...Scattered cloud cover, calm winds, and moist ground has aided in patchy fog development this morning as of 11Z Thu, resulting in a mix of VFR and LIFR conditions within portions of the Willamette Valley. Expect these deteriorated conditions at various terminals, mainly the southern Willamette Valley, to continue this morning and likely improve/clear back to VFR by 19-21Z Thu. Light offshore winds at KAST and KONP should be enough to prevent fog development at these TAF sites. As for KTTD and KPDX, easterly winds in the Gorge may prevent low stratus/fog development, however current obs showing winds at 5 kt or less gives moderate to low confidence that stratus will stay out of these terminals. Nonetheless, guidance only suggests a 20% chance of MVFR CIGs at KPDX and KTTD through 19Z Thu. Near the end of the TAF period, around 09-12Z Fri, there is a 30-50% chance for a return of deteriorated conditions, likely MVFR according to the latest guidance.

Overnight lows continue to fall into the low to mid 30s early this morning, so there may also be some frost development over metal surfaces. If a terminal frosts out, fog development would be less likely to occur.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Light and variable winds around 3-4 kt continue this morning, aiding in possible fog and/or frost development as temperatures cool into the low to mid 30s. Guidance suggests a 20% chance of MVFR CIGs through 18Z Thu. Expect mostly VFR conditions through the TAF period, with the exception of a 20-30% chance of MVFR CIGs near the end of the TAF period, around 09-12Z Fri. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Building high pressure will maintain northerly winds less than 20 kt today. The westerly swell will also subside, bringing seas down to 7-9 ft at 12-13 seconds by this afternoon. As a result, the current Small Craft Advisory over all of the waters will come to an end by 10 AM today. Winds turn more southerly on Friday ahead of the next system, but gusts remain below 20 kt. Seas also fall to 6-7 ft by the end of the week.

The next system arrives late Friday night into Saturday, returning breezy southerly winds and small craft wind gusts up to 30 kt. There is also a 20-30% chance for isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt across the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore and a 10-20% chance for the inner waters and Columbia River Bar. Seas gradually build over the weekend as another westerly swell moves in, with high confidence (>80%) for seas building again to 10 ft or greater, and a 30-40% chance for seas of 15 ft or greater. ~12/10
